note: Facts and sources behind the member descriptions in OH.json, gathered 2026-10-05. "review" holds research notes for a human check; "issues" lists open questions.

byways.name: Amish Country Byway
byways.designation: Ohio Scenic Byway; National Scenic Byway (America's Byway)
byways.where: Double loop on SR 39, US 62 and connecting roads through Holmes County and neighboring Tuscarawas, Wayne and Knox counties; Loudonville, Millersburg, Berlin, Walnut Creek, Sugarcreek

facts.fact: Holmes County holds Ohio's largest Amish settlement, founded in 1808; the Amish make up about half the county's population.
Tour stops include the Walnut Creek covered bridge, the Behalt cyclorama of Amish and Mennonite history, Guggisberg Cheese and the weekly Mt. Hope auction.
ODOT's byway layer gives the route as 196.4 miles and flags it as one of America's Byways.

byways.review: ODOT's current line (196.4 mi) is about twice the catalog line (76 mi); the former Gateway to Amish Country byway (catalog gateway-to-amish-country-69094) lies wholly on the current ODOT line and appears to have been absorbed.

byways.name: Appalachian Byway
byways.where: SR 78 from Clarington on the Ohio River through Woodsfield, Caldwell and McConnelsville to Nelsonville; Monroe, Noble, Morgan and Athens counties

facts.fact: The byway starts on SR 78 at Clarington in Monroe County, where it meets the Ohio River Scenic Byway, and ends in Nelsonville in Athens County.
Stops include the Thorla-McKee oil well, the USS Shenandoah airship memorial, the Big Muskie dragline bucket and Burr Oak State Park.
Nelsonville's square is lined with the town's own Star Brick.

byways.review: The catalog's Morgan County Scenic Byway (morgan-county-scenic-byway-13594) lies entirely on this route and covers roughly half of it; it appears to have been merged into the Appalachian Byway.

byways.name: Big Darby Plains Scenic Byway
byways.where: Union County roads along Big Darby Creek: Plain City, Unionville Center, Milford Center, North Lewisburg

facts.fact: The main route runs beside the state and nationally designated scenic Big Darby Creek for more than 27 miles.
Union County's covered bridges on the route include Reuben Partridge's 1868 Culbertson bridge and the 2006 Buck Run bridge, called Ohio's longest single-span wooden bridge.
Small pioneer cemeteries kept as prairie preserves hold royal catchfly, which blooms from late July through August.

byways.name: Drovers' Trail Scenic Byway
byways.where: SR 800 from Hendrysburg to Barnesville, then SR 147 to Bellaire on the Ohio River; Belmont County

facts.fact: The route follows SR 800 between Hendrysburg and Barnesville and SR 147 from Barnesville to Bellaire.
It recalls nineteenth-century cattle drives and links the Historic National Road with the Ohio River Scenic Byway in 37 miles.
Dysart Woods along the way is a 51-acre tract of original oak forest with trees 300 to 400 years old; Woodside Farm still shows the trench of the old drove road.
The route ends at Bellaire near the Great Stone Viaduct, a mid-1800s railroad structure on the National Register.

byways.name: Granville Scenic Byway
byways.where: About 10 miles from SR 37 by James Road north onto SR 661 through Granville; Licking County

facts.fact: The route begins at SR 37, meets James Road and continues north on SR 661.
The Buxton Inn, built in 1812, is described as Ohio's oldest inn still standing.
Alligator Mound, an effigy mound about 200 feet long, sits above the village, and Denison University's Swasey Chapel crowns College Hill.

byways.name: Heritage Corridors of Bath
byways.where: Township roads linking the hamlets of Ghent, Bath Center and Ira; Bath Township, Summit County, next to Cuyahoga Valley National Park

facts.fact: Roadways connect nineteenth-century hamlets with mills, cemeteries, a nature preserve and the national park.
The Ghent Woolen Mill of 1832 is called the oldest surviving woolen mill in Ohio, and nearby stands an 1859 two-story octagonal bee house.
Hale Farm and Village, with more than ten buildings from 1825 to 1850, lies on Oak Hill Road at the end of the route.

byways.name: Historic National Road
byways.where: US 40 across the state, 225 miles from Bridgeport on the Ohio River through Zanesville, Columbus and Springfield to the Indiana line

facts.fact: In Ohio the byway runs 225 miles from the West Virginia line at the Ohio River to the Indiana line.
The 1828 Blaine Hill S Bridge over Wheeling Creek is the oldest documented standing bridge in Ohio.
Ohio's Madonna of the Trail statue, west of Springfield, was the first of twelve and was dedicated by Harry S. Truman in 1928.
The road is lined with pike towns that grew up around stopping points; the Red Brick Tavern at Lafayette hosted several presidents.

byways.name: Hocking Hills Scenic Byway
byways.designation: Ohio Scenic Byway; National Scenic Byway (America's Byway)
byways.where: SR 374 (with SR 56) from South Bloomingville to Rockbridge on US 33, around Hocking State Forest; Hocking County

facts.fact: The byway follows SR 374 through the Hocking Hills and around Hocking State Forest.
Ash Cave's sandstone rim spans 700 feet, with a waterfall dropping 90 feet; Conkle's Hollow is walled by Blackhand Sandstone cliffs up to 240 feet high.
ODOT notes that the byway has been named one of America's Byways.

byways.review: Now a National Scenic Byway (ODOT page and Wikipedia's national list); the catalog lists it only as an Ohio State Scenic Byway.

byways.name: Jefferson Township Scenic Byway
byways.where: Clark State Road, Reynoldsburg-New Albany Road, Kitzmiller Road and others in Jefferson Township, Franklin County, east of Columbus

facts.fact: The byway shows older barns and homes, many from the early 1800s, with streams and stands of trees.
A house of 1832 on Clark State Road served as the toll keeper's house when that road was the main route toward Newark and Granville.
Kitzmiller Road hugs Blacklick Creek, where water mills once stood.

byways.review: ODOT names it simply 'Jefferson Township' (layer) or 'Jefferson Township Byway' (page).

byways.name: Johnny Appleseed Historic Byway
byways.where: About 40 miles on SR 39 and connecting roads from Loudonville through Perrysville and Lucas to Mansfield and Mifflin; Ashland and Richland counties

facts.fact: The byway runs more than 30 miles along SR 39 and celebrates John Chapman, the orchardist and nurseryman.
A recorded 1826 lease near Loudonville gave Chapman half an acre to plant fruit, with the rent paid in 20 apple trees.
Stops include Mansfield's square, the Copus monument of 1882 and Louis Bromfield's Malabar Farm.

byways.name: Lake Erie Coastal Ohio Trail
byways.designation: Ohio Scenic Byway; National Scenic Byway (America's Byway)
byways.where: About 293 miles along the Lake Erie shore from the Pennsylvania line (US 20, Conneaut) through Cleveland, Sandusky and Toledo to Waterville

facts.fact: The 293-mile byway passes beaches, state parks, lighthouses, vacation islands and villages as well as big cities.
The glacial grooves on Kelleys Island are 400 feet long and up to 15 feet deep.
Stops include the Ashtabula Harbor Lighthouse, Magee Marsh, Crane Creek and the Old Woman Creek estuary.

byways.name: Land of the Cross-Tipped Churches
byways.where: About 38 miles of county and state roads among Catholic villages in Mercer, Auglaize, Shelby and Darke counties: Maria Stein, Minster, Fort Loramie, St. Henry, Coldwater

facts.fact: The 38-mile route is lined with cross-tipped churches listed on the National Register of Historic Places, in farm country settled early.
St. Michael's at Fort Loramie, dedicated in 1881, has a tower more than 200 feet tall built of over a million bricks.
Swiss-born architect Anton DeCurtins and his sons designed many of the churches; the Shrine of the Holy Relics at Maria Stein grew from an 1844 convent.

byways.review: ODOT layer and page show 47.4 miles; brochure says 38. Catalog line (14 vertices) covers only about a third of ODOT's line.

byways.name: Lincoln Highway Historic Byway
byways.where: About 241 miles across northern Ohio on US 30 and older Lincoln Highway alignments: East Liverpool, Lisbon, Canton, Wooster, Mansfield, Bucyrus, Lima, Van Wert

facts.fact: Ohio's portion of the Lincoln Highway, begun in 1913 as the first coast-to-coast road, is 241 miles long.
Brick stretches of the original highway survive on Cindell and Baywood streets east of Canton.
Stops include the Lincoln Highway pillars at Crestline and the Kewpee hamburger diner in Lima.

byways.review: Catalog line covers roughly two thirds of ODOT's line.

byways.name: Lower Valley Pike Scenic Byway
byways.where: About 11 miles of Lower Valley Pike (CR 316) along the Mad River west of Springfield to Medway; Clark County

facts.fact: The byway follows County Road 316 for about 11 miles.
The Mad River runs beside it under limestone cliffs, with woods and wetlands.
Jacob Huffman spent seven years building his limestone house from 1825; nearby is the site of the 1780 battle at Peckuwe.

byways.review: ODOT calls it 'Lower Valley Pike' (layer) or 'Lower Valley Pike Byway' (page).

byways.name: Maumee Valley Scenic Byway
byways.where: About 90 miles along both banks of the Maumee River from Defiance through Napoleon, Grand Rapids, Waterville, Maumee and Perrysburg to Rossford; Defiance, Henry, Wood and Lucas counties

facts.fact: The 90-mile route begins in Defiance at SR 15 and River Drive.
War of 1812 sites include Fort Meigs; Fallen Timbers battlefield of 1794 is also on the route.
At Providence Metropark visitors ride a reproduction mule-drawn canal boat; Side Cut Metropark keeps three locks of the canal's side cut.

byways.review: ODOT shows 89.5 miles; brochure says nearly 60.

byways.name: Miami & Erie Canal Scenic Byway
byways.where: About 55 miles following the old canal from Piqua (Johnston Farm) through Lockington, Fort Loramie, Minster, New Bremen, St. Marys and Spencerville to Delphos; Miami, Shelby, Auglaize and Allen counties

facts.fact: At Lockington five stone lift locks once raised boats 67 feet.
Grand Lake St. Marys was built as a canal feeder reservoir and still supplies the canal through a three-mile feeder.
New Bremen's Lockkeeper's House visitor center stands on the Towpath Trail in a region settled by Germans.

byways.review: ODOT calls it 'Miami and Erie Canal' (layer) or 'Miami and Erie Canal Byway' (page).

byways.name: Neil Armstrong Scenic Byway
byways.where: Streets of Wapakoneta, Auglaize County, along the route of the 1969 homecoming parade

facts.fact: The route through downtown Wapakoneta retraces Neil Armstrong's homecoming parade after the moon landing.
The Armstrong Air & Space Museum, built to look like a moon base, opened on July 20, 1972.
Armstrong earned his student pilot certificate at 16 at the Port Koneta field, before he had a driver's license.

byways.name: North Ridge Scenic Byway
byways.where: SR 254 (Detroit Road and North Ridge Road) through Avon and Sheffield Village, about 9 miles; Lorain County

facts.fact: The byway covers the whole of SR 254 in Lorain County and passes more than a hundred historic homes.
It follows the northernmost ancient beach ridge across Avon and Sheffield.
Avon was once called the Greenhouse Capital of America; the 1840s Hurst stone house is nicknamed the Stone Eagle.

byways.name: Ohio & Erie Canalway
byways.designation: Ohio Scenic Byway; National Scenic Byway (America's Byway)
byways.where: About 110 miles from Cleveland through Cuyahoga Valley National Park, Akron, Massillon and Zoar to New Philadelphia, with a spur to Canton

facts.fact: The 110-mile byway runs from Cleveland to New Philadelphia within the Ohio & Erie Canalway National Heritage Area, with a spur from Massillon to Canton.
At Canal Fulton the mule-drawn boat St. Helena III gives rides on a restored stretch of canal.
Stops include Hale Farm, the Cascade Locks in Akron, Zoar Village and Fort Laurens, Ohio's only Revolutionary War fort site.

byways.name: Ohio River Scenic Byway
byways.designation: Ohio Scenic Byway; National Scenic Byway (America's Byway)
byways.where: About 452 miles of SR 7 and US 52 along the Ohio River from East Liverpool through Marietta, Gallipolis and Portsmouth to Cincinnati; 14 counties

facts.fact: The byway spans 14 counties and the whole Ohio length of the river, 452 miles.
East Liverpool, the start, was built on pottery. The Fly ferry to Sistersville, West Virginia, in business since 1815, is the only ferry joining Ohio and West Virginia.
Portsmouth's floodwall murals cover about 2,000 feet; the Rankin House at Ripley was an Underground Railroad station.

byways.name: Old Mill Stream Scenic Byway
byways.where: US 224 and SR 37 along the Blanchard River from Mt. Blanchard through Findlay, Gilboa and Ottawa to Glandorf; Hancock and Putnam counties

facts.fact: The byway follows the Blanchard River along US 224 and SR 37 in Putnam and Hancock counties.
It takes its name from the song 'Down by the Old Mill Stream' and passes through Findlay, Flag City USA.
The Great Karg gas well came in at Findlay on January 20, 1886, and its flame burned for more than four months.

byways.review: Catalog line covers about 60 percent of ODOT's line.

byways.name: Quaker Heritage Scenic Byway
byways.where: About 54-mile loop between Waynesville and Wilmington by way of Caesar Creek; Warren and Clinton counties

facts.fact: The 54-mile loop traces the Quaker migration into Ohio.
Waynesville's white brick Miami Meetinghouse of 1811 is described as the oldest continuously used religious building west of the Alleghenies.
Caesar Creek's 1849 meetinghouse was moved to Pioneer Village when the lake was built; Isaac and Sarah Harvey went from here to see Lincoln about emancipation in 1862.
The 1811 meetinghouse has two doors and two equal sides for men's and women's meetings; the Caesar Creek spillway is a fossil-hunting ground.

byways.review: Brochure places it in southeast Ohio, but ODOT's storymap and layer put it in southwest Ohio (Warren and Clinton counties). ODOT's layer name is 'Quaker Heritage Scenic Byway'; the storymap calls it 'Quaker Historic Byway'.

byways.name: Scenic Olentangy Heritage Corridor
byways.where: SR 315 from I-270 in Franklin County north along the Olentangy River to US 23 in Delaware County, about 10 miles

facts.fact: The corridor begins at I-270 and follows the Olentangy River to US 23.
SR 315 was the first road commissioned in Delaware County, in 1808.
Highbanks Metro Park is named for a 100-foot shale bluff over the Olentangy State Scenic River, which runs east of and parallel to SR 315; stone houses and the Bieber Mill line the road.

byways.review: ODOT now calls it 'Olentangy Heritage Corridor'.

byways.name: Scioto Heritage Trail
byways.where: Loop roads from Portsmouth west through Shawnee State Forest to Otway and Rarden and back by Duck Run and Lucasville; Scioto County

facts.fact: The byway begins in downtown Portsmouth and joins the Ohio River Scenic Byway near the floodwall murals.
It passes the boyhood homes of Roy Rogers and Branch Rickey, plus remnants of the Ohio and Erie Canal.
Otway's covered bridge dates from 1874, and the route runs through Shawnee, Ohio's largest state forest.

byways.review: ODOT now calls it 'Scioto Heritage Trail'.

byways.name: Tappan-Moravian Trail Scenic Byway
byways.where: About 55 miles on US 250, SR 799 and county roads around Tappan and Clendening lakes, with a northern loop by SR 646 through Scio and Jewett; Harrison and Tuscarawas counties

facts.fact: The 55-mile byway winds past Tappan Lake and around Clendening Lake through rural eastern Ohio.
When Tappan Dam was built, Pleasant Valley Church and its graves were moved up the hill and the Brownsville church was moved from the abandoned village of Tappan.
New Rumley is the birthplace of George Armstrong Custer.

byways.review: ODOT page slug is misspelled 'tappen-moravian-trail-byway' but works.

byways.name: Wally Road Scenic Byway
byways.where: Wally Road (old Walhonding Valley rail bed) from Loudonville south along the Mohican River to Greer; Ashland, Holmes and Knox counties

facts.fact: The road uses the old bed of the 'Wally', the Toledo, Walhonding Valley and Ohio railway, in Mohican River country.
Loudonville calls itself the Canoe Capital of Ohio for its many liveries on the Mohican.
The hamlet of Greer was a stop on the railroad; a one-room Walnut Grove School of the late 1800s was restored in 2002.

byways.review: ODOT line is about 10 miles; catalog covers about half of it.

byways.name: Welsh Scenic Byway
byways.where: Loop through Gallia and Jackson counties: Gallipolis, Rio Grande, Centerville, Oak Hill, Jackson

facts.fact: The loop through Gallia and Jackson counties honors Welsh immigrants who settled southeastern Ohio in the nineteenth century.
Many Welsh chapels on the route have two front doors and a tea house, or ty capel, for feeding the minister.
Welsh settlers built charcoal iron furnaces; Buckeye Furnace is a restored example.

byways.review: ODOT line is 64.4 miles; catalog line (45 mi) covers under half of it.

byways.name: Covered Bridge Scenic Byway
byways.where: SR 26 from Marietta to Woodsfield along the Little Muskingum River; Washington and Monroe counties

facts.fact: The byway follows SR 26 from Marietta to Woodsfield, mostly beside the Little Muskingum River.
A self-guided tour covers 35 miles with ten marked stops and four campgrounds along the way.

byways.review: Not part of ODOT's Ohio Byways list.

issues: Catalog roads not in ODOT's current list of 27: Accommodation Line Scenic Byway (Waynesville to Spring Valley, US 42; only ~20% overlaps the Quaker Heritage byway), Jefferson County Scenic Byway (Jefferson County near Smithfield), Presidential Pathways Ohio Scenic Byway (western Hamilton/Butler counties, US 27 area). They look de-designated; left out of the chapter.

Gateway to Amish Country (gateway-to-amish-country-69094) lies wholly on ODOT's current Amish Country Byway line, which is now 196.4 miles versus the catalog's 76; the catalog ACB line covers under half of the current route. Consider redrawing ACB from ODOT layer 0 (Byway_Name = 'Amish Country Byway') and retiring the Gateway entry.

Morgan County Scenic Byway (morgan-county-scenic-byway-13594) lies wholly on the Appalachian Byway (SR 78) and covers about half of it; looks merged. Appalachian Byway is given bywayId null with gisValue; consider retiring the Morgan County entry.
Hocking Hills Scenic Byway is a National Scenic Byway (ODOT page; Wikipedia's national list, 2021 round); the catalog flags it as state-only.
Brochure describes Quaker Heritage Scenic Byway as southeast Ohio, but its route and storymap are in southwest Ohio (Waynesville, Wilmington).

Brochure abbreviations are sloppy (Welsh labeled OEC, Hocking Hills labeled HCB in one place); lengths disagree across sources for Maumee Valley (60 vs 89.5 mi), Land of the Cross-Tipped Churches (38 vs 47.4), Amish Country (160 vs 196.4), Appalachian (105 vs 122.3).

Catalog lines cover only part of ODOT's line for Welsh (~42%), Wally Road (~48%), Old Mill Stream (~58%), Lincoln Highway (~67%), Historic National Road (~70%), Land of the Cross-Tipped Churches (~36%); could be redrawn from ODOT layer.
Facts cite ODOT StoryMap URLs; the text was read from the arcgis.com item data JSON for each story because the story pages render client-side.
